analysis.one_liner: Limits secret court settlements that hide information about public health and safety hazards.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a House vote; it sat in the Judiciary Committee and its courts subcommittee until the 112th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: When companies settle lawsuits, the settlements often include secrecy orders that hide evidence of dangerous products, drugs, or practices — even from safety regulators. This bill would stop federal courts from approving such secrecy unless the judge makes a specific finding that confidentiality outweighs the public's interest in knowing about the hazard. It would also guarantee that parties can always share relevant information with federal and state regulators, and it would protect personal privacy with a presumption favoring confidentiality for individuals' personal data.
analysis.who_benefits: Consumers, patients, and workers who could be harmed by products or practices whose dangers were documented in lawsuits but kept secret by settlement. Regulators and journalists who would gain access to hazard information currently buried in sealed files.

how_it_helps.text: Bars courts from approving settlements or protective orders that hide information about public health or safety hazards unless the judge first finds, on the record, that confidentiality outweighs the public interest in disclosure [S2, S3].

Guarantees that parties to a case can always disclose relevant information to any federal or state agency that regulates the activity at issue, so regulators are not cut off by settlement terms [S2, S3].

Lets parties publicly disclose that a settlement was reached and discuss the health or safety issues in the case (though not the dollar amount paid), unless a judge makes the same narrow findings [S2, S3].
Includes a rebuttable presumption that protecting a person's personally identifiable information outweighs public disclosure, addressing the privacy objection [S2, S3].

analysis.who_pays: Corporations facing lawsuits over product safety — drug makers, device makers, manufacturers — would lose their ability to settle quietly and keep hazard evidence out of public view, which could make cases harder to settle and raise litigation costs.

drawbacks.text: Blanket limits on confidentiality can make defendants less willing to settle, which means longer, costlier litigation for injured plaintiffs and slower compensation [S3].

Broad hazard-disclosure rules can sweep in legitimate trade secrets and business information; the bill handles personal privacy with a presumption but leaves companies to argue case-by-case that a 'specific and substantial' confidentiality interest justifies secrecy [S3].

Opponents of similar measures have argued courts already balance these interests under existing rules, making a statutory mandate unnecessary; the bill did not advance far enough for that argument to be tested in hearings or on the floor [S1, S5].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core benefit is real: lawsuits have repeatedly documented hazards — defective products, unsafe drugs — that stayed hidden from regulators and the public because of settlement secrecy, and this bill directly targets that. The costs are manageable by design: judges can still order secrecy with specific findings, dollar amounts stay confidential, and personal privacy is presumed protected. The main risk is chill on settlements, which the drafters accepted in exchange for public safety transparency.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to the House Judiciary Committee, which sent it to a subcommittee, and no hearing, markup, or floor vote ever happened before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Jerrold Nadler introduced the bill on February 9, 2011; it was referred to the House Judiciary Committee the same day [S1, S5].
On February 14, 2011, it was referred to the Subcommittee on Courts, Commercial and Administrative Law, where it remained [S5].
Three Democratic representatives cosponsored the bill [S4].
No further action — no markup, no floor vote, no Senate companion action recorded in the bill's history — occurred before the 112th Congress ended on January 3, 2013 [S1, S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Corporations that benefit from confidential settlements over health and safety hazards are better off; the public gained nothing from the bill's death.

for.name: Rep. Jerrold Nadler
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Sunshine in Litigation Act of 2011 and led support for it.

against.name: House Judiciary Committee leadership
against.role: Committee with jurisdiction over the bill
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a hearing or markup on the bill after referring it to a subcommittee.

sides.party_line_note: There was no vote, so no split can be measured; all identified support was Democratic, and the bill died in committee without a recorded opponent.

industries.note: The bill would prevent settlements from sealing evidence of drug or device hazards from regulators and the public. Companies could no longer resolve safety lawsuits quietly with the danger details buried.

industries.industry: Product manufacturers and their liability insurers
industries.note: Confidential settlement terms are a common tool for resolving products liability cases without public admissions. The bill would require judges to find a specific confidentiality interest before approving such terms, raising settlement difficulty and litigation costs.
